fact: The Synthetic Turf Council says permeable synthetic grass systems are typically designed to drain 25 inches of water per hour, and that the turf and its base should drain fast enough for local weather and rainfall.
quote: Synthetic grass systems with infill and base materials should drain to accommodate local weather and rainfall patterns. Permeable synthetic grass systems are typically designed to drain 25” of water per hour. … A contract that specifies base preparation details. The water permeability rate for the base materials and the synthetic grass should be high enough to accommodate the local weather and rainfall patterns;
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Considerations When Buying Synthetic Grass for Landscape Use (September 2013)
notes: Read from the PDF with pdftotext on 2026-09-25 (dated September 2013; still the guideline the STC serves). A trade association guideline, not a test standard: the page says "typically designed", never that any product meets it.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, a turf distributor, says its hole-punched landscape turfs drain at over 30 inches per hour per square yard, flow-through backings drain at hundreds of inches per hour, and non-permeable backings, never advised for lawns, are common on putting green and bocce turf because those dense, heavily infilled surfaces make ordinary drainage very difficult.
quote: A non-permeable backing does not allow water to pass through the turf and into the base. This type of turf backing is never advised for landscape applications, but it is commonly found in synthetic grass products specifically made for putting green and bocce ball use. This is because both games require a very dense turf and high quantities of infill, making traditional drainage very difficult to incorporate. … all drain at a rate of over 30 inches per hour per square yard. … This results in an unprecedented drainage rate of hundreds of inches per hour.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How Does Backing Quality Affect Your Artificial Turf's Drainage? (Feb. 28, 2023)
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. The 30 in/hr figure is for the distributor's own 13 Pic, 15 Pic and K29 hole-punched lines, not the industry; say "one distributor". pet-turf-vs-regular-turf.sgw-backing-types quotes the same article on backing types.

fact: ForeverLawn's K9Grass Classic+ specification requires the installed turf and drainage system to pass water at not less than 800 inches per hour, recommends a permeability test of the sub-base, and calls for a base of clean 3/8 to 5/8 inch angular stone, with any mix over 20% fines approved by the maker.
quote: The installed synthetic grass and drainage system shall allow for drainage and water flow through the system at a rate of not less than 800” per hour. … Recommend there is drainage/water permeability test of sub-base. … Installation of the free draining base aggregate of 3/8” to 5/8” clean compactable angular stone (any mix with fines in excess of 20% must be approved by manufacturer), shall follow procedures provided.
source_label: ForeverLawn, K9Grass Classic+ dog-specific outdoor surface specifications, 1.2.C, 1.3 and 3.1.C (M1266 Rev. 03/22)
notes: Read from the PDF with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. A dog-specific, no-infill product; named as a published example, not a recommendation. Its auxiliary-drainage sentence is pet-turf-vs-regular-turf.k9grass-classic-plus-subbase.

fact: In NRCS soil survey data for Larimer and Weld counties and the Longmont area, the slowest layer of Nunn clay loam passes water at about 0.13 inches an hour once saturated and its surface layer at about 0.2 to 0.4, while Olney fine sandy loam passes about 1.3 in its slowest layer and about 3.3 at the surface.
quote: SSURGO major components, survey areas CO644, CO617, CO618 and CO643 (hydgrp · ksat_r of the slowest horizon · ksat_r of the surface horizon, micrometers per second): Nunn clay loam (CO644 73, 74, 75; CO618 41, 42; CO643 NuA, NuB, NuC; CO617 41) — C · 0.915 · 1.41 to 2.82; Olney fine sandy loam (CO617 44, 45; CO618 46, 47, 48) — B · 9 · 23
source_label: USDA-NRCS Soil Data Access (SSURGO), component hydrologic group and saturated hydraulic conductivity (ksat_r), survey areas CO644, CO617, CO618 and CO643
notes: Queried 2026-09-25 (SELECT on legend, mapunit, component and chorizon; major components only). Inches per hour are our arithmetic: micrometers per second × 0.1417 (3,600 s per hour ÷ 25,400 micrometers per inch): 0.915 → 0.13; 1.41 → 0.2; 2.82 → 0.4; 9 → 1.3; 23 → 3.3. Ksat is how fast a saturated soil layer transmits water, not a site measurement: soils vary lot to lot, and fill on new lots is not mapped. CO644 Larimer County Area, CO617 Weld County Southern Part, CO618 Weld County Northern Part, CO643 Boulder County Area.

fact: CSU Extension's simple drainage test is a hole 12 inches deep filled with water: if it has not drained in 30 minutes the soil has a drainage problem, and if it has not drained in 24 hours waterlogged soil may affect plant growth.
quote: A simple test to evaluate soil drainage is to dig a hole twelve inches deep and fill it with water. If the water fails to drain in thirty minutes, the soil has a drainage problem. If the hole fails to drain in twenty-four hours, waterlogged soils may affect plant growth.
source_label: CSU Extension, Soil Drainage (CMG GardenNotes #219; reviewed September 2022)
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. A garden-soil test; the page presents it as a screen before turf, not as a base-design method.

fact: CSU Extension says water is slow to move, or may not move at all, in compacted soils and soils over 20% clay, and that in many Colorado soils water soaks into the upper layers only to stop at a less permeable layer below.
quote: In comparison, soils dominated by small-sized pores (i.e., compacted soils and soils with greater than 20% clay content), water is slow to move or may not move at all. … Poor drainage is a common problem in many Colorado soils. In some areas, the upper layers of soil allow water infiltration only to have the water stopped as it reaches a less permeable subsurface soil layer.
source_label: CSU Extension, Soil Drainage (CMG GardenNotes #219; reviewed September 2022)
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25.

fact: CSU Extension says many surface drainage problems come from over-irrigation, and that soil around new homes is typically compacted by construction traffic.
quote: Irrigation – Many surface drainage problems arise from over-irrigation (too much and/or too often). Compaction – Compaction is difficult to deal with; so, prevention is the key. Soils around new homes is typically compacted from construction traffic.
source_label: CSU Extension, Soil Drainage (CMG GardenNotes #219; reviewed September 2022)
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25.

fact: CSU Extension describes a French drain as a rock-filled trench, usually with a pipe, that must slope at least 1 to 3% to an outlet, suggests filling a low spot or installing a drain with a gravity-flow outlet for standing water, and says drain tile works only as far as the soil lets water reach it and the water can flow downhill to an outlet.
quote: A French drain is a lined ditch-like trench that is filled with rock or gravel, typically with a pipe in the bottom. It catches water runoff and directs it away from structures that can be damaged. The rock should meet grade to prevent soil from covering the drain. The trench must slope at least 1-3% and flow to an outlet. … Standing water – It is common to find standing water in low spots. Fill in the low spot or install a French or underground drain with a gravity-flow outlet. … Use of soil drainage tiles are only effective to the extent that the soil will allow water to flow through it to the drain tile, and water in the drain tile can flow downhill to an outlet.
source_label: CSU Extension, Soil Drainage (CMG GardenNotes #219; reviewed September 2022)
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25.

fact: PolyTurf's landscape installation manual says turf over clay or hard-packed soil will not drain on a level surface, and where drainage is an issue calls for a perimeter trench about 12 inches deep and 12 inches wide backfilled with aggregate as a drainage sump.
quote: For example, if the sub-strate is clay or extremely hard, packed soil, it will not drain on a level surface. … If drainage is an issue- Around the perimeter, the substrate should be dug out to a depth of about 12” deep by 12” wide, and then backfilled with the aggregate to provide a drainage sump.
source_label: PolyTurf, Installation and Maintenance Instructions: Synthetic Grass for Landscaping (site preparation)
notes: Read from the PDF with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. A California maker's manual; its base material names (Class 2 Aggregate Base) are California specs, so the page cites only the clay and sump sentences.

fact: Firestone's code says installing artificial turf may not impede or alter a lot's drainage pattern, and requires a compacted, porous aggregate base at least 3 inches deep so water drains both horizontally and vertically without excessive runoff or pooling.
quote: ii. The drainage pattern of the lot shall not be impeded or altered by the installation of artificial turf. iii. Artificial turf shall be installed over a compacted and porous aggregate base material that is a minimum of three (3) inches deep to allow for adequate drainage both horizontally and vertically and to prevent excessive runoff or pooling.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.e.ii–iii (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read through the Municode API (api.municode.com CodesContent, jobId 488870, productId 18062) on 2026-09-25; the library page renders by script. The base depth is also in firestone-fdc-16.6.4-turf-specs.

fact: Colorado 811 says homeowners must contact it before digging even a small hole, and that its free locates do not mark privately owned utilities.
quote: Even if your digging project is small, it is always required to contact 811! … Remember, “privately owned utilities” won’t be included in this service.
notes: Read from the raw HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. The same page says state law requires contact at least two full business days before digging and, in its steps, to wait at least 3 full business days; the guide gives no day count.

fact: FieldTurf's landscape care guide says leaves left on turf over winter can decompose into a layer of organic matter that impedes drainage and encourages moss.
quote: Autumn: As leaves begin to fall, it’s important to remove them regularly. If left to sit over winter, they can decompose and create a layer of organic matter that can impede drainage and encourage moss growth.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide
